opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing that it's a "move away" from language. I've spent most of my career on language, and I still think language is one of the most remarkable things about human intelligence. But over the last few years it's become increasingly clear to me that language alone isn't the whole story.

If you think about how a child learns, they don't start from text. They spend years looking at the world, poking at things, dropping them, seeing what happens, and language gets layered on top of that grounded experience. Words like "behind," "pour," or "fragile" only really mean something because you have a model of how objects and space and physics work. Large language models have done astonishingly well by soaking up the statistical traces of all that in text, honestly far better than I or most people in NLP expected. But you also see the gaps: they can talk fluently about the world while getting basic spatial or causal reasoning wrong in ways no four-year-old would.

So for me it's less a change of field than following the question where it leads. If you care about meaning and understanding, which is what drew me to linguistics in the first place, you eventually have to ask what the words are *about*. That pushes you toward perception, toward vision, and toward models that maintain some internal representation of how the world is and how it changes, which is roughly what people now mean by world models.

There's also a practical side. The interesting frontier now is systems that act, agents that operate in environments, use interfaces, or manipulate things. For that, a purely textual understanding falls short. You need models that can see, that can predict the consequences of actions, and that can connect all of that back to language so humans can communicate with them. To me, language and visual understanding are two halves of the same problem, and the exciting work is in bringing them together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses language, visual understanding, and world models, but does not mention early visual question answering models answering from prior expectations rather than image information.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd push back gently on the framing, because I don't think of it as moving away from language so much as following where the questions about meaning actually lead you.

For a long time in NLP we were essentially working with text as a closed system. You learn the distribution of words, you learn how they co-occur, and remarkably, you get a lot of mileage out of that. That was the whole story of distributional semantics, and then of the large language models, which are really distributional semantics scaled up by many orders of magnitude. And one of the surprising things of the last several years is just how much you can learn about the world from text alone. People used to say, you can't learn what the color red is from text, and it turns out you can learn a very large amount about red from text.

But there's a limit. Language is a very compressed, very lossy report on the world. When I say "the cup fell off the table," there's an enormous amount of physical and causal structure behind that sentence that the sentence itself doesn't carry. Human language is efficient precisely because speakers assume the listener already has a model of how objects, people, and causes behave. So if you care about meaning, which I always have, at some point you have to ask where that underlying model comes from.

Children are the obvious case. A child has spent a couple of years watching things fall, pushing things, seeing people come and go, before they produce much language at all. The language gets grounded onto a world model that's already quite rich. And I think the interesting scientific question, and now also the practical one, is whether machine systems can build something like that from perceptual experience, especially video, and then have language sit on top of it rather than language trying to do all the work.

So for me it was a fairly natural progression. Vision and language had been getting closer for a decade anyway, with image captioning, visual question answering, and then the multimodal models. What's changed recently is that the models are good enough that you can seriously ask about prediction and simulation, about systems that anticipate what happens next in a scene, rather than just labeling what's in it. That's what people mean by world models, and I find it compelling because it loops back to the original question of what it means to understand something. I don't think you understand a sentence in any deep sense unless you can connect it to a model of situations, and the situations are ultimately out there in the physical and social world, not in the text.

r001.rationale: The response mentions visual question answering as part of the field’s progression, but does not say early models often relied on prior expectations instead of image information.

astra-6.text:
For me, it’s less a move away from language than a widening of the question. If you’re interested in language understanding, you eventually have to ask: what is the language about? People are talking about objects, events, intentions, and things that happen in the world. Understanding those descriptions seems to require some understanding of the world itself.

Language gives you an enormous amount of indirect evidence. But vision offers another way to connect concepts to things—to see objects, how they relate to one another, and how a situation changes over time. And that leads naturally to the question of world models: can a system do more than recognize what’s in front of it? Can it predict what might happen next, or how taking an action would change things?

So I see these as closely connected problems. The broader ambition is to understand how you build systems that connect language, perception, and action into a coherent understanding of the world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses vision as a way to connect concepts to objects and situations, but does not say early visual question answering models often relied on prior expectations rather than image information.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it more as a broadening of the language question than a move away from it. If you’re interested in how language conveys meaning, you eventually have to ask what that meaning is grounded in. We use language to talk about objects, events, intentions, and how the world changes. There’s a tremendous amount you can learn from text, but text doesn’t explicitly spell out all of that background knowledge.

Vision gives you another way into the problem. You can connect words with things you observe, and with video you can start to connect descriptions with actions and changes over time. That leads naturally to the question of world models: can a system learn enough about how things work to anticipate what might happen next, or what would happen if it took a particular action?

So the continuity, for me, is understanding. Language is an extraordinarily powerful source of evidence about the world, but it makes sense to study it alongside perception and action.

r001.rationale: The response discusses connecting words to visual observations, but does not say that early visual question answering models often relied on prior expectations instead of the image.
